description: North Macedonia's national e-services portal, in use since December 2019, reached 338 services by the end of August 2026, including partly available ones, and the Commission reports that its usage rate doubled from the previous year, after the most-demanded certificates went online in 2025. The rise starts from a low level of use, the rate is not defined, and the Commission links it to the new services only by saying that the two went together.
problem_addressed: North Macedonia's portal was little used: the State Audit Office found 0.556 requests per registered user and that visually impaired persons could not use it (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0194; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0026, machine translated), the Commission recorded 292,179 users but only 2,070 applications a month in 2024 (MKD-EU-2024-001-0024), and 78 institutions still offered 1,120 services only in person (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0055, machine translated). The Commission said in 2024 that the most commonly requested services were not yet online (MKD-EU-2024-001-0021) and in April 2026 still called digital government quite underdeveloped, with most e-services rarely used and only a fraction fully transactional (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007). The audit attributes low use to citizens' weak interest, insufficient promotion and equal prices for electronic and paper documents (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0006, machine translated).
reform_or_mechanism: The portal (uslugi.gov.mk) rests on the 2019 Law on Electronic Management and Electronic Services (INT-MKD-0035) and was upgraded through an EU-funded project to add services, first for businesses and then those most demanded by citizens (INT-MKD-0125; MKD-EU-2025-001-0135). The Reform Agenda sets a payment step to increase the offer of e-services by 50% by June 2027 (INT-MKD-0101; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0091). The long-term ICT strategy SMART/MK plans mandatory integration or connection of each e-service on the portal and a change in the price of e-services (INT-MKD-0489; INT-MKD-0523; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0194; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0197, machine translated), and an analysis for DigInfo centres to support users (INT-MKD-0355; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0127, machine translated). Single Sign-On was integrated across service providers by 2026 (INT-MKD-0317; MKD-EU-2026-007-0098).
how_implemented: Offered: the portal has been in use since December 2019 (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0032, machine translated). Counts differ by source and definition: 392 or 264 at the 2024 baseline, 124 accessible online by September 2024, 314 in the 2025 strategy, and 338 at the end of August 2026 including partly available ones, given as 336 in another chapter of the same report (MKD-EU-2024-008-0013; MKD-GOV-2024-001-0092; MKD-EU-2024-001-0072; MKD-GOV-2025-004-0068; MKD-EU-2026-007-0021; MKD-EU-2026-007-0086). Upgrade: in 2024 the Commission reported only a few new services and the long-awaited 135 not yet configured (MKD-EU-2024-001-0021; MKD-EU-2024-001-0023); in 2025 services for businesses, an easier user interface and new services mostly demanded by citizens, including birth, marriage and citizenship certificates (MKD-EU-2025-001-0135; MKD-EU-2025-001-0136); and in 2026 new services for citizens and businesses (MKD-EU-2026-007-0099). The Reform Agenda step, mandatory integration, the price change and the DigInfo centres remain plans, and progress against the 50% target cannot be fixed because the baselines conflict. Capacity: the audit found 101 of 242 posts for the platform unfilled (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0076, machine translated), and the Commission described ownership as fragmented, with limited resources for the lead ministry (MKD-EU-2023-003-0045).
evidence_of_results: Used: the Commission states that the growth in services 'was accompanied by a growing usage rate, which doubled from the previous year' (MKD-EU-2026-007-0022), and that 2025 and early 2026 saw significant improvements in digitalisation while service delivery still requires efforts to meet EU standards (MKD-EU-2026-007-0019). The starting level was low: about 13 of 100 people aged 18 to 70 were registered on the portal according to the 2025 strategy (MKD-GOV-2025-004-0075, machine translated). A search of all 4,629 passages in the North Macedonian evidence files for usage, user, application, request and end-to-end wording found no count of applications or users after 2024 other than that registration share, which states no reference date, and no share of portal services completed online end to end; the Commission says only that a fraction are fully transactional (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007). Who is served: the Commission says the portal caters for people with special needs (MKD-EU-2024-001-0020; MKD-EU-2026-007-0020), which conflicts with the audit's finding that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0136, machine translated), and in 2026 it finds that digital divides leave rural and older women behind and asks for compliance with accessibility standards (MKD-EU-2026-007-0130; MKD-EU-2026-007-0104).
limitations_of_evidence: The usage rate has no stated definition, base, figure or origin, so the doubling cannot be placed on a scale; the April 2026 statement that most e-services are rarely used describes the level, and the November statement describes the change (MKD-EU-2026-003-0007; MKD-EU-2026-007-0022). The Commission states the link between new services and use only as co-occurrence, and Single Sign-On integration and an easier interface came in the same period (MKD-EU-2026-007-0098; MKD-EU-2025-001-0135). Service counts are not comparable across sources, and the 338 includes partly available services. The audit and strategy figures are machine translated and capped at Medium confidence. The North Macedonian evidence was gathered for the earlier country study and its 2026 update; North Macedonia's own assessments are context, not evidence about Moldova. The finding that the upgrade was implemented was made before the 2026 report and has not yet been revisited in its light. Claims of absence in this case rest on searches of all North Macedonian evidence passages in the project, not of the full source texts.
practical_lesson: Agent synthesis, not stated by a source: in North Macedonia, use of the portal rose in the year the services citizens most often request went online, after years in which a growing count of rarely requested services left use low. Moldova's remaining gap sits in a similar place: 61% of citizen services are digitalised against 82% for businesses (MDA-EU-2026-012-0117), and rural demand, which the Commission found low in 2025, rose significantly in 2026, including in rural areas where 118 service centres were set up to respond to persistently low demand (MDA-EU-2025-001-0045; MDA-EU-2026-012-0039). The case suggests ranking further digitalisation by how often citizens request a service, and testing the audit's stated causes of low use, promotion and the price of electronic against paper documents; Moldova's own strategy already proposes lower fees for digital services (MDA-GOV-2023-001-0059).
transferable: As a conditional hypothesis only: putting the most-requested citizen services online end to end and checking use after each addition, promoting the portal, and giving electronic documents a price advantage over paper ones. Moldova already reports the share of services digitalised separately for citizens and businesses, so use could be followed as citizen services are added (MDA-EU-2026-012-0117). The account of causes rests on one audit, machine translated, and the rise in use on one unexplained Commission sentence.
not_transferable: North Macedonia's improvement starts from a narrower range than Moldova's: 338 services including partly available ones, against 636 on EVO of which 447 are online (MDA-EU-2026-012-0038), so the gain from each added service may be smaller in Moldova. Levels of use cannot be compared: a search of all 3,686 Moldovan evidence passages in the project for usage wording found only figures defined differently from North Macedonia's, such as the share of public service users who accessed services electronically (MDA-GOV-2025-003-0173) and active users of the EVO application (MDA-GOV-2026-002-0042). North Macedonia's main constraint is a short-staffed lead ministry, whereas Moldova's government names a cost of digitalisation above its own resources (MDA-GOV-2024-004-0044). Moldova has already set up 118 centres for rural users (MDA-EU-2026-012-0040), where North Macedonia offers only a planned analysis of DigInfo centres, so the case says nothing about assisted access. The Reform Agenda conditions differ: North Macedonia's counts e-services offered, while Moldova's open condition counts services integrated in the EVO Sign wallet (MDA-EU-2025-002-0035).
notes: New case for RUN-2026-02 (P4 step 5), built from validated RUN-2026-01 items and judgements on RI-TEC-036@MKD (direction JDG-011083, gap JDG-011084; implementation statuses JDG-009052, JDG-009341, JDG-009056, JDG-009201, JDG-011463, JDG-009326, JDG-009045, JDG-009003), reused without new collection (E19, LIM-0048). Every intervention already has a validated status, so no new status is proposed. The implementation status of the upgrade (JDG-009341, implemented) carries a rereview flag from GATE-0012 and predates the 2026 report.

description: Albania placed most services on e-Albania, with a 2023 law obliging institutions to use it, and an international source reports high use. Full transactions are not established, payment often fails, and no extracted item shows that the law or the portal caused the reported use.
problem_addressed: Albania's gap is reported mainly as depth and inclusion: the Commission records 95% of applications for 1,237 services offered online in 2024 and 1,253 in 2025, yet accessibility for vulnerable groups remains unaddressed. The sources conflict on range, because the RCC also says Albania 'continues to lag behind the regional average in certain aspects of service scope and sophistication', with a citizen services score of 50 against 53 from desk research in 2025. It also asks Albania to improve access to the use of e-services and to address an emerging digital divide. The national monitor finds digitalisation largely complete but citizens not at the centre of design and delivery.
reform_or_mechanism: Law No. 43/2023 on Electronic Governance, adopted in June 2023, requires public institutions to use e-Albania as the primary point of access and requires e-payment through the portal; as stated in the sources, the duty falls on institutions, not users. The Digital Agenda 2022-2026 sets a 95% target. ADISA was absorbed by the National Agency for Information Society, which concentrates policy and operational control.
how_implemented: Offered: the monitor records more than 90% of services placed on the portal since its previous cycle and most physical counters closed, while municipal offices still handle services that need in-person steps. Fully transactional: no extracted item gives a national count, and of seven sampled services the monitor calls two end-to-end, while its own footnote says the payment option usually does not work, and others, such as vehicle registration and VAT, need in-person payment. No service is yet delivered as a life event. Vehicle registration and VAT are described as offered outside the portal in one passage and as sampled services needing in-person payment in another.
evidence_of_results: Used: the Regional Cooperation Council (RCC) reports e-government users at 78.5% of internet users in 2023 and 88.6% in 2024, with 3.43 million registered users and 15.2 million services provided in 2024 and 17 million in 2025. The monitor's perception survey has 66.9% agreeing that they can access services easily online and 30.5% disagreeing. No extracted item gives the share of those services that were completed online from start to finish.
limitations_of_evidence: The RCC gives no origin for the portal figures and does not define a registered user or a service provided; its text says 89% of the population where its table says 88.6% of internet users. The e-government user indicator counts any online contact with authorities, not portal use (ALB-IO-2026-001-0046). The extracted items hold no series from before the June 2023 law, so use before and after it cannot be compared. The monitor's informant scores are points awarded only if all informants agree (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0078; 0 of 3 on accessible service delivery, 3 of 3 on ease of use), so they are not counts of people. The monitor states that 'these reforms explain why' informants describe transactional reliability and ease of access (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0006), but this rests on three informants, concerns their views and not use, and conflicts with its footnote that payment 'usually does not work' (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0043). The monitor also reports the law's once-only duty both ways, as effectively implemented (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0017) and as partial (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0010, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0057, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0059, ALB-CSO-2025-001-0065); these items sit in the unmatched queue, stay unused under G5b and are listed for the analyst. Claims of absence in this case refer to the extracted items, not the full source text.
practical_lesson: This case was built for North Macedonia; its lesson for Moldova is stated in the transferability judgement below.
transferable: The monitor reports that absorbing ADISA into the agency removed one named overlap, on monitoring, evaluation and reporting between ADISA and the Agency for Dialogue and Co-governance (ALB-CSO-2025-001-0080; ALB-CSO-2025-001-0076). This is a narrow result with no measure, and North Macedonia already has a lead ministry that lacks resources and cooperation (MKD-EU-2023-003-0045), so naming one body would not by itself address its problem. A legal duty on institutions to integrate services is an untested option: no extracted item shows that it caused Albania's range, and Albania's experience shows that working payment and signature cannot be assumed.
not_transferable: Closing counters cannot be assumed to transfer: the source gives no count, date or effect on users, and North Macedonia has 1,120 services available only in person and an audit finding that persons with disabilities cannot use e-services (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0055; MKD-GOV-2024-007-0136, both machine translated). Albania's own unaddressed accessibility issues show that its route has not solved this. Relative size was not assessed because no extracted item gives it. In these items the Commission's ask of Albania is a recommendation, while North Macedonia's increase in e-services is also a Reform Agenda condition (MKD-EU-2024-007-0015).
notes: Case reused from RUN-2026-01 (validated at its G6b), unchanged; comparator relevance and transferability judged afresh for Moldova.

description: Montenegro launched a new portal in December 2024 and a plan for transactional services, but sampled core services were not on it and use on the broad indicator fell before it launched. This case is too early and unverified, and its delivery figures rest on the government's own report.
problem_addressed: Montenegro's government names low use of e-services and weak interoperability as key challenges, and the Commission repeatedly asks it to prioritise a platform for transactional services. The national monitor reports that the government's own Digital Services Plan 2025-2027 puts no service at the fifth level (full online service). E-government users were 37.5% of internet users in 2024, below the Western Balkans average of 54%.
reform_or_mechanism: Sources date the new eUprava portal differently in kind: the government adopted an information note on it in December 2024, when the monitor says it 'was not functional'; the Commission and the event report say it launched that month; and first services were published in April 2025. It runs under a plan for transactional services 2025-2027 covering 171 services and 21 institutions, revised on 18 December 2025; the RCC says the same plan sets out 162 additional services and the revised plan's table sums to 175, and these figures are not reconciled. The Law on Electronic Government gives the legal basis, and the government launched an initiative for all institutions to publish their services on the portal. A proposed Open Government action plan targets 150 transactional services by 2029.
how_implemented: Offered: the government reports 106 services from 14 institutions on the portal, without saying how many are transactional, and eFirma and eTaxis run outside it. Fully transactional: the government's action plan states 45 transactional services (MNE-GOV-2025-001-0009), while its Digital Services Plan 2025-2027, as cited by the monitor, puts no service at level 5 (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0012). These are two government statements not shown to be at the same date (the action plan is dated 12 October 2025; the monitor, dated September 2025, does not date the plan's state of play), not reconciled, and no extracted item holds an independent count of transactional services. Delivery against the plan was 25 of 57 by July 2025, then 57 of 57 on the government's own report, with no independent check in the extracted items. The ministry reports two officials in the responsible directorate, a refusal of budget reserve for Interior services and Employment Agency services waiting on a new law. The ministry's report on the Digital Transformation Strategy gives 43.14% of planned 2024 activities fulfilled, for the whole strategy and not only e-services (government reporting, machine translated; repeated by the monitor, MNE-CSO-2025-001-0031).
evidence_of_results: Used: e-government users fell from 48.4% of internet users in 2023 to 37.5% in 2024, on an indicator of any online contact with authorities (ALB-IO-2026-001-0046), and an oral UNDP figure puts actual use at 8%. No extracted item gives use of eUprava itself. The monitor's service delivery grades reflect findings to the end of 2024, when the portal was under construction (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0028; MNE-CSO-2025-001-0027). Its statements that information improved and that none of the seven sampled services was on the portal are notes made at the time of writing, after the first services of April 2025. The government states that satisfaction is around 50%.
limitations_of_evidence: The portal is young. The monitor, a non-government body co-funded by the monitored ministry (SQ-00180), sets its findings to the end of 2024, when the portal was under construction, with later notes to July 2025 (MNE-CSO-2025-001-0028; MNE-CSO-2025-001-0027), so its grades largely predate the first services, and the government's report of full delivery and the 106 count are untested. The RCC text says use continues to grow, against the fall in its own table. The 8% figure is oral, second-hand and has no reference period, and the event report is rated Low. The 2024 user figures predate almost all of the portal's life, so they measure the starting position. The 106 services, 25 and 57 of 57, the 43.14%, the two officials, the budget refusal and 'key challenges' come from machine-translated Montenegrin government reports, capped at Medium; they are not legal texts, so they are outside LIM-0029 as worded, for the analyst to confirm at G6b, and item MNE-GOV-2025-002-0008 is also flagged possible_misread. Claims of absence in this case refer to the extracted items, not the full source text.
practical_lesson: This case was built for North Macedonia; its lesson for Moldova is stated in the transferability judgement below.
transferable: As a conditional hypothesis only: a portal may add little where the services people need sit elsewhere, and North Macedonia's Commission findings say the most commonly requested services are not yet online (MKD-EU-2024-001-0021). It rests on one monitor and seven sampled services, whose grades largely predate the first services, that monitor also reports a gain in information, and no extracted item measures use of eUprava. The stated constraints of too few staff and refused budget have a parallel in North Macedonia's unfilled posts and limited resources for the ministry (MKD-GOV-2024-007-0076; MKD-EU-2023-003-0045).
not_transferable: The Montenegrin portal launched in December 2024 on the Commission's account, while North Macedonia's has run since 2019 (MKD-GOV-2023-002-0021) and has a longer record of low use, so results at Montenegro's stage may not predict results at a later one. The cybersecurity crisis that the Commission dates to 2023 and says delayed services and eroded trust (the government's action plan refers instead to 'the 2022 attacks', MNE-GOV-2025-001-0004, classed out_of_scope at pass 2) has no stated equivalent in North Macedonia's evidence here. Montenegro's different accession stage was not used as a reason, because no extracted item links it to the portal.
notes: Case reused from RUN-2026-01 (validated at its G6b), unchanged; comparator relevance and transferability judged afresh for Moldova.
